content: 1. Individuals who have received the pertussis vaccine within the past year may exhibit elevated IgG levels, which can persist for over a year following infection or vaccination. This can lead to potential false-positive results in serological testing. 2. Culture and PCR testing are more specific and reliable methods for detecting acute pertussis infections compared to serology. These methods are preferred for accurate diagnosis. 3. A confirmed case of pertussis can be established through laboratory testing or epidemiological linkage. Laboratory confirmation involves either isolating Bordetella pertussis or detecting its genomic sequences via PCR, provided the PCR meets performance criteria. 4. Alternatively, a laboratory-confirmed case can be identified in individuals aged 11 years or older who exhibit elevated IgG antibodies to pertussis toxin at least one year after their last vaccine dose. 5. An epidemiologically linked case is defined as a person meeting the suspected case definition who has had close contact with a laboratory-confirmed case (or another epidemiologically linked case in an outbreak setting) within three weeks prior to the onset of cough. 6. Close contact is defined as face-to-face exposure to a case, including household or family contact, sharing a room overnight with a case, or direct contact with respiratory, oral, or nasal secretions of a laboratory-confirmed case. 7. A clinically compatible case refers to a suspected case that meets the pertussis case definition but lacks laboratory confirmation due to either the inability to collect a sample or negative test results. 8. A discarded case is a suspected case that does not meet the pertussis case definition. 9. Contact tracing should prioritize high-risk contacts, such as infants, pregnant women in their third trimester, healthcare workers caring for infants or pregnant women, and individuals living or working with infants. 10. Only symptomatic contacts of confirmed cases should be tested for pertussis. Asymptomatic contacts should not undergo testing, and testing should not be a criterion for post-exposure prophylaxis decisions. 11. Post-exposure antimicrobial prophylaxis (PEP) is not always an effective use of public health resources. However, if resources allow, asymptomatic contacts may receive PEP within 21 days of the index patient’s cough onset to prevent symptomatic infection. 12. When pertussis is strongly suspected, close contacts should be identified and provided with preventive treatment without waiting for laboratory confirmation. 13. Antibiotics are most effective in preventing or mitigating pertussis when administered during the incubation period or early catarrhal stage. During the paroxysmal phase, antibiotics do not alter the clinical course but can eliminate bacteria from the nasopharynx, reducing transmission. 14. Suspected cases should avoid contact with young children and pregnant women in late pregnancy, especially those who are unimmunized, until they have completed at least five days of antibiotic treatment. 15. Hospitalized patients with pertussis should be placed under respiratory isolation or, at a minimum, follow contact and respiratory droplet precautions, such as wearing a mask around others. 16. Natural infection does not provide long-lasting immunity against pertussis. Patients recovering from clinical pertussis who have not completed their primary vaccine series should receive the necessary doses to complete the series or an age-appropriate booster dose if indicated. 17. An outbreak is defined as an increase in pertussis cases or incidence above the baseline in a specific geographical area. This requires local judgment to determine. 18. Pertussis outbreaks can be challenging to identify and manage due to the periodic nature of the disease (increased rates every 3–5 years) and the presence of other respiratory pathogens with similar symptoms. 19. Epidemiological investigations during outbreaks can provide valuable insights into vaccine effectiveness and the epidemiology of pertussis, including case distribution and fatality rates by age group. 20. High-severity outbreaks among infants may indicate gaps in immunization coverage, while outbreaks in older age groups may suggest waning immunity or changes in surveillance practices. 21. Active case searches should be conducted promptly after identifying a suspected case, ideally within 48 hours of confirmation. This includes assessing household, neighborhood, workplace, or school contacts for illness. 22. Surveillance systems should ensure consistent monitoring of trends over time. Countries may rely on epidemiological linkage to reduce the burden on laboratories during outbreaks. 23. All reporting sites must immediately notify health authorities of suspected pertussis cases, including patient identifiers and contact details. Weekly reports should be submitted, even if no cases are observed, to confirm the operational status of the surveillance system. 24. Each suspected case should be assigned a unique identification number (UID) that includes geographical location, year, and serial number. All communications and forms related to the case should reference this UID. 25. Data analysis should include time and place analysis to detect changes in disease incidence, clustering of cases, or silent areas. Mapping cases on a local map over time can help identify spatial clustering and guide interventions. 26. Vaccination efforts should focus on undervaccinated individuals who have had contact with pertussis cases. Vaccination may not prevent illness in those already infected, and immunity from vaccination or prior infection wanes over time. 27. New data suggest that immunity from acellular pertussis vaccines wanes significantly within 2–3 years, particularly in individuals who have not received whole-cell vaccine doses.
